title: Least Squares
goal: This chapter sets up the linear model in matrix form and fits it by minimizing the sum of squared residuals. It is the foundation of the book: ch02 changes the normal equations derived here to make the fit stable.

objectives.text: After this chapter you can write a regression problem in matrix form, give the shapes of \(X\), \(w\) and \(y\), and compute the residual vector.
objectives.why_core: Every later section and both chapters' exercises use this notation.

objectives.text: After this chapter you can derive the normal equations from the squared loss and state when they have a unique solution.
objectives.why_core: ch02 modifies these equations (§2.2), and exercises 1.2–1.3 depend on them.

objectives.text: After this chapter you can explain the least-squares fit as an orthogonal projection and use the orthogonality of the residual.
After this chapter you can choose a numerically stable solver instead of the explicit inverse and explain why.

map.title: The model
concepts: Design matrix \(X\) (n × d): samples as rows, features as columns
Prediction vector \(Xw\) and the intercept column of ones

map.title: The squared loss
concepts: \(L(w) = \|y - Xw\|^2\): differentiable, symmetric, large errors weigh more
Link to Gaussian noise and maximum likelihood

map.title: The normal equations
concepts: Gradient \(-2X^\top(y - Xw)\) and the normal equations \(X^\top X w = X^\top y\)
Unique solution iff the columns of \(X\) are linearly independent; requires \(n \ge d\)

map.title: Geometry of the fit
concepts: \(X\hat w\) as the orthogonal projection of \(y\) onto the column space
Residual orthogonal to every column; residuals sum to zero with an intercept
Adding a feature never increases the training error

map.title: Computing the solution in practice
concepts: Forming \(X^\top X\) squares the condition number

quiz.prompt: For \(n\) samples described by \(d\) features, without an intercept, what are the shapes of \(X\), \(w\), \(y\) and of the residual \(r\)?
quiz.solution: \(X\) is \(n \times d\), \(w\) has \(d\) entries, \(y\) has \(n\) entries. The prediction \(Xw\) has \(n\) entries, so the residual \(r = y - Xw\) has \(n\) entries too: one per sample.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about the least-squares residual \(r = y - X\hat w\) is always true?

options.why: \(r\) is zero only if \(y\) already lies in the column space of \(X\); in general the model cannot reach \(y\).

options.text: \(r\) is orthogonal to every column of \(X\).
options.why: The normal equations say \(X^\top(y - X\hat w) = 0\).
A common mix-up: the residual is orthogonal to the fitted vector \(X\hat w\), not to \(y\).

options.text: Each entry of \(r\) is as small as possible in absolute value.
options.why: Least squares minimizes the sum of squares; individual residuals can be larger than under other fits.

quiz.solution: The normal equations can be read as an orthogonality condition: \(X^\top r = 0\), so \(r\) is perpendicular to every column of \(X\), and hence to every vector in the column space, including the fit \(X\hat w\).

quiz.prompt: Let \(X = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 1 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(y = (1, 2, 4)^\top\). Compute \(\hat w\) from the normal equations, then check that the residuals sum to zero.
quiz.solution:
\(X^\top X = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 3\\ 3 & 5\end{pmatrix}\) and \(X^\top y = (7, 10)^\top\). The determinant is \(15 - 9 = 6\), so \(\hat w = \tfrac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix}5 & -3\\ -3 & 3\end{pmatrix}(7, 10)^\top = (5/6,\ 3/2)^\top \approx (0.833, 1.5)\).

Predictions: 0.833, 2.333, 3.833. Residuals: 0.167, −0.333, 0.167, which sum to zero because \(X\) has a column of ones.

quiz.prompt: A colleague computes the weights with `np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y` on data where two features are almost identical. What would you change in the code, and why?
quiz.solution: Replace the explicit inverse with `np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)`. Nearly identical features make the problem ill-conditioned, and forming \(X^\top X\) squares the condition number, so rounding errors are amplified. `lstsq` works on an orthogonal factorization of \(X\) and avoids that step.

quiz.prompt: "If \(X^\top X\) is invertible, the explicit-inverse formula and `lstsq` always return numerically identical weights."
quiz.solution: False. The two formulas are mathematically equal whenever \(X^\top X\) is invertible, but they are different algorithms. On well-conditioned data they agree to many digits; on ill-conditioned data the explicit inverse loses accuracy and the results can differ noticeably.

quiz.prompt: Explain, with the geometry of §1.4, why adding a feature to \(X\) can never increase the training sum of squared residuals.
quiz.solution: The fit is the projection of \(y\) onto the column space of \(X\). Adding a column can only enlarge that subspace, and the closest point of a larger subspace is at least as close to \(y\) as the closest point of the smaller one, because the old fit is still available. Hence the squared distance from \(y\) — the training sum of squared residuals — cannot increase.

glossary.definition: The n × d matrix whose rows are samples and whose columns are features.
The gap between observed targets and predictions for a given weight vector.
The sum of squared residuals, minimized by least squares.
The linear system obtained by setting the gradient of the squared loss to zero.
The set of all linear combinations of the columns of \(X\), where every prediction lives.
The closest point of a subspace to a vector; the error is perpendicular to the subspace.
A measure of how much a problem amplifies small errors in its data; forming \(X^\top X\) squares it.
